microstructure: Predominantly soft ferritic iron with localized carburized areas around 0.2–0.3 wt% carbon and rarer areas around 0.4–0.8 wt%.
limits: Average hardness combines heterogeneous sampled areas and is not a finished-object performance test. Local carburized zones do not make the whole bloom uniform steel.

microstructure: Generally ferritic; one small patch of mild steel around 0.1–0.3 wt% carbon was observed near a surface.
limits: The bar came from a quarter of one bloom and is nonuniform in size and shape. Its higher average hardness cannot isolate cold forging from sampling or represent ancient iron generally.

microstructure: Ferritic iron with pyrrhotite and slag inclusions; the slower charging experiment did not produce the expected steely bloom.
limits: Five hardness points describe one experimental sample. The failed prediction about carbon shows why operating variables cannot be converted into a universal recipe.

microstructure: Ferritic iron with intergranular wüstite and pyrrhotite inclusions.
limits: The authors observed breaking and splitting during forging. Average hardness does not measure toughness forgeability service life or finished-tool performance.

microstructure: Predominantly soft ferritic iron with slag inclusions.
limits: This is the lowest mean bloom hardness in the four-run series but had better workability. It is not evidence that softer iron is universally better.

microstructure: Ferritic bar with wüstite glass and pyrrhotite slag inclusions.
limits: Five measurements on one nonstandard bar cannot be compared directly with finished ancient weapons tools or bronze objects.

microstructure: Ferritic iron with sulfur-rich pyrrhotite inclusions; the higher hardness was linked to phosphorus rather than carbon steel.
limits: The hardest mean bloom in this series was also difficult to forge. Hardness is not toughness quality or technological superiority.

microstructure: Ferritic bar with pyrrhotite inclusions and a major forging crack; sulfur and phosphorus decreased relative to the bloom.
limits: The hardness decrease and chemistry change may reflect oxidation and material breaking away. The row does not quantify total forging loss or finished-object reliability.
